results.summary: The design forms a coherent SageMaker-centered ML deployment pipeline with explicit training, registry-based versioning, gated deployment, A/B traffic splitting, monitoring, and retraining feedback.

findings.title: Immutable lineage and versioned promotion are well integrated
findings.explanation: The pipeline ties data manifests, preprocessing outputs, training runs, experiment records, and registry entries together, which gives strong traceability from input to deployed model.

findings.title: A/B testing is supported directly at the serving layer
findings.explanation: The multi-variant endpoint with traffic splitting is a clear and sufficient mechanism for controlled model comparison.

findings.title: Operational feedback loop is closed
findings.explanation: CloudWatch metrics can trigger retraining through the workflow, so monitoring does more than observe; it also feeds the retraining path.

results.summary: The design presents a coherent AWS ML deployment pipeline with versioned training, registry-based promotion, multi-variant serving, automated retraining, and operational monitoring aligned to the published core scope.

findings.title: No material core gaps identified
findings.explanation: The submitted architecture covers the end-to-end ML pipeline scope: training, validation, registry-backed versioning, API serving, A/B testing, monitoring, automated retraining, and scalable inference. The latency and throughput constraints are addressed through warm capacity and autoscaling on the serving endpoint, while lineage and experiment tracking are explicitly modeled.

results.summary: The design provides a coherent AWS ML pipeline with versioned training, gated promotion, multi-variant serving, monitoring, and automatic retraining, and its serving path is aligned with the stated latency and throughput constraints.

findings.title: Managed pipeline covers the full ML lifecycle
findings.explanation: The architecture connects preprocessing, training, experiment tracking, registry promotion, deployment, online serving, monitoring, and retraining into one durable workflow.

findings.title: A/B traffic splitting is explicitly supported at the serving layer
findings.explanation: The multi-variant endpoint includes traffic splitting for controlled comparison, which directly matches the A/B testing requirement without requiring a separate experimentation service.

findings.title: Low-latency serving path is thoughtfully shaped
findings.explanation: Prediction requests go through API Gateway to a warm, autoscaling SageMaker endpoint, while the API measures full request-to-response latency. That is a coherent strategy for the under-100ms objective.

results.summary: The design covers the ML deployment pipeline end to end with versioned training, registry-backed promotion, A/B serving, monitoring, and automated retraining; remaining gaps are mainly in cost control, trigger specificity, and operational clarity.

findings.title: Autoscaling strategy is present but not explicitly bounded for the requested throughput
findings.explanation: The endpoint autos-scales on request load and saturation, which is directionally correct for 1000+ predictions/sec, but the submission does not specify scaling limits, instance sizing, or concurrency behavior that would show how the design stays stable at that load.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit scaling policy details such as target metrics, min/max capacity, and concurrency assumptions so the throughput target is operationally credible.

findings.title: Warm-capacity inference strategy may raise serving cost
findings.explanation: The endpoint is intentionally kept warm for the latency objective and can split traffic across variants. That supports performance, but it also implies ongoing capacity spend that is not balanced with an explicit cost-control mechanism for low-traffic periods.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit cost-aware serving policy such as scale-to-zero for noncritical environments, scheduled warm-capacity tuning, or variant right-sizing based on observed load.

findings.title: Inference path depends on an assumed low-overhead API front door
findings.explanation: API Gateway fronts the prediction path and forwards to the endpoint, which is coherent, but the design does not spell out how request validation, serialization, and backend invocation overhead stay within the under-100ms budget under peak load.
findings.recommendation: Specify payload limits, connection reuse, and timeout budgets for the API-to-endpoint path so the latency target remains credible at peak traffic.

findings.title: Security posture is implied rather than fully spelled out
findings.explanation: The API is described as authenticated and validated, and S3 uses access-controlled versioned prefixes with encryption, but the endpoint- and registry-side access boundaries are not described in the same level of detail.
findings.recommendation: Clarify IAM/service-role boundaries for registry updates and endpoint invocation so the trust model is explicit end to end.

findings.title: Retraining trigger conditions need operational definition
findings.explanation: Monitoring can start qualified retraining, but the design does not state the drift or schedule thresholds that determine when retraining is triggered, which makes the automation path partially underspecified.
findings.recommendation: Define the retraining trigger policy, including drift thresholds, alert routing, and any debounce or approval rules.

findings.title: Deployment automation is gated but rollback behavior is not explicit
findings.explanation: The workflow can apply a reviewed endpoint configuration after checks pass, but the submission does not describe what happens when deployment or post-deployment validation fails, which leaves the automation path incomplete.
findings.recommendation: Specify rollback and failed-deployment handling, including how the registry rollback reference is used to restore the prior serving version.

findings.title: A/B traffic split criteria are not fully parameterized
findings.explanation: The endpoint supports traffic splitting for comparison, but the submission does not describe how split ratios are selected, rolled back, or promoted based on experiment outcomes.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit traffic-split and promotion rules, including rollback conditions and success metrics, to make A/B testing operationally complete.

findings.title: Monitoring coverage is good but alert actionability is not explicit
findings.explanation: CloudWatch metrics include latency, errors, saturation, variant metrics, and drift indicators, which is a strong observability foundation; however, the alerting/decision thresholds that turn metrics into actions are not detailed.
findings.recommendation: Define alarm thresholds, dashboards, and which metric combinations trigger retraining or rollback to make operations more actionable.

findings.title: Serve-and-compare architecture is appropriate for the requested scale
findings.explanation: The multi-variant endpoint with autoscaling and warm capacity directly addresses the need to scale inference endpoints while preserving fast comparison traffic.

findings.title: Lineage is captured end to end across data, code, and artifacts
findings.explanation: The registry and experiment store preserve run IDs, digests, evaluation evidence, and rollback references, which supports lineage and repeatability well.

results.summary: A coherent global CDN design centered on CloudFront, with S3 for static origin, a dynamic application origin, Lambda@Edge location logic, ACM-backed HTTPS, Shield protection, and CloudWatch monitoring.

findings.title: Edge delivery path is coherent and complete
findings.explanation: The design routes viewers through Route 53 to CloudFront, then fans out to S3 for static assets and the dynamic origin for eligible dynamic requests. This matches the global CDN scope and keeps browser traffic on the CDN delivery path rather than exposing origins directly.

findings.title: Security controls align with the public delivery surface
findings.explanation: HTTPS termination via ACM on CloudFront plus Shield protection on the same public endpoint provides the expected baseline for secure global delivery and DDoS mitigation.

findings.title: Operational visibility is integrated into the existing stack
findings.explanation: CloudFront metrics and Lambda@Edge telemetry flow into CloudWatch, which gives a practical observability path for cache performance, delivery behavior, and edge-function execution.

results.summary: A coherent AWS CDN design is provided with CloudFront at the center, supported by Route 53, S3, a dynamic origin, Lambda@Edge customization, ACM TLS, Shield protection, and CloudWatch telemetry.

findings.title: Global CDN path is coherently assembled
findings.explanation: The design has the essential viewer, DNS, CDN, origin, customization, security, and monitoring pieces connected in the right direction for a global content delivery system.

findings.title: Edge customization is scoped through Lambda@Edge
findings.explanation: Location-aware behavior is implemented as an edge function rather than by duplicating content paths, which matches the brief's customization requirement while preserving the CDN delivery model.

findings.title: HTTPS delivery is explicitly terminated at the CDN
findings.explanation: Viewer HTTPS is supported by the CloudFront distribution and ACM-backed certificate attachment, providing a clear TLS path for client traffic.

findings.title: Operational visibility includes delivery and edge telemetry
findings.explanation: CloudFront metrics and Lambda@Edge telemetry are routed to CloudWatch, giving the design a concrete monitoring path for cache behavior and edge execution.

results.summary: A coherent AWS CDN design with CloudFront, S3 and dynamic origins, Lambda@Edge personalization, ACM-backed HTTPS, Shield protection, and CloudWatch monitoring that covers the published core scope.

findings.title: CloudFront-centric delivery path is well aligned to the brief
findings.explanation: The architecture routes all viewer traffic through CloudFront, separates static and dynamic origins, and adds location-aware edge logic, TLS, DDoS protection, and monitoring. This matches the published core scope closely.

results.summary: The design cleanly uses CloudFront, S3, Lambda@Edge, Route 53, ACM, Shield, and CloudWatch to satisfy the legacy CDN brief with a coherent global delivery path, edge caching, location-aware customization, HTTPS, DDoS protection, invalidation support, and cache monitoring.

findings.title: Global CDN path is coherent and complete
findings.explanation: The architecture has the core delivery chain needed for a global CDN: DNS resolution to Route 53, viewer traffic to CloudFront over HTTPS, static content from S3, dynamic content from the application origin, and location-aware logic through Lambda@Edge.

findings.title: Security and operational controls are aligned with the brief
findings.explanation: HTTPS viewer delivery, ACM-managed certificate attachment, and Shield protection on the public CDN endpoint directly address the request for encrypted access and DDoS protection.

findings.title: Observability covers the required cache-performance signal
findings.explanation: CloudFront telemetry flowing into CloudWatch, plus Lambda@Edge telemetry, provides a reasonable basis to monitor cache performance, origin request volume, and edge behavior.

results.summary: A coherent global CDN design using Route 53, CloudFront, S3, a dynamic origin, Lambda@Edge, ACM, Shield, and CloudWatch that covers the published core scope and constraints.

findings.title: Edge-delivery architecture is well aligned with the brief
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates DNS, global CDN delivery, static origin, dynamic origin, edge customization, TLS, DDoS protection, and monitoring. That combination directly supports the published CDN scope without unnecessary architectural baggage.

findings.title: Cache-performance observability is explicitly covered
findings.explanation: CloudFront delivery metrics and Lambda@Edge telemetry flow into CloudWatch, which is sufficient to observe cache behavior, viewer latency, and edge execution without adding redundant monitoring components.

results.summary: The design covers the core compliance, audit, threat detection, reporting, remediation, and retention flow well, but it still needs explicit mapping to PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and SOC 2 and a confirmed in-scope account boundary.

findings.title: Compliance standards are not explicitly mapped to PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and SOC 2
findings.explanation: The design has the right building blocks for compliance monitoring, but it does not show how Config rules, evidence reports, or remediation policies are aligned to the three named standards. That leaves the standards requirement only partially demonstrated rather than fully evidenced.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit control mappings or rule groups for PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and SOC 2, and show how reports express pass/fail evidence for each framework.

findings.title: Approved account scope and exclusions still need confirmation
findings.explanation: The account-boundary component says account membership, regions, and exclusions remain to be confirmed. That does not break the architecture, but it means the exact coverage boundary for recording, auditing, and remediation is still unresolved.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the in-scope organization units, regions, and any excluded accounts/resources before implementation.

findings.title: Centralized evidence pipeline is well structured
findings.explanation: CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, Security Hub, EventBridge, SNS, S3 Object Lock, and SSM Automation form a coherent end-to-end flow for collection, detection, notification, archive retention, and remediation.

results.summary: A coherent AWS data lake design that ingests structured and unstructured data, catalogs and governs it, queries in place with Athena, and publishes dashboards through QuickSight.

findings.title: None material; architecture is internally coherent for the published scope
findings.explanation: The submitted design covers ingestion, raw storage, cataloging, governed SQL access, transformation, and visualization with an appropriate AWS lake toolchain. The current evidence does not show a core-scope contradiction or missing required component.

results.summary: A coherent AWS lakehouse-style design covers multi-source ingestion, raw and curated storage, automated cataloging, governed SQL access, and dashboarding with a clear in-place query path.

findings.title: Governed lake query path is well-structured
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates raw landing, transformation, cataloging, governance, query, and visualization responsibilities. Athena reads curated S3 data through Glue Catalog metadata, while Lake Formation mediates access.

findings.title: Ingestion paths cover both streaming and batch sources
findings.explanation: The architecture accepts replayable streams through Kinesis/Firehose and batch/file/database extracts directly into raw S3, which matches the multi-source lake scope.

results.summary: The design presents a coherent AWS data lake with raw and curated S3 zones, automated cataloging, governed in-place SQL via Athena, and QuickSight visualization, matching the published core scope.

findings.title: End-to-end lake pattern is coherent and scope-aligned
findings.explanation: The submitted architecture covers ingestion, raw retention, transformation, cataloging, governed SQL access, and dashboard consumption using AWS-native lake services. The component responsibilities and data flow are internally consistent and directly match the published core scope.

findings.title: Governance is wired through both query and metadata paths
findings.explanation: Lake Formation is connected to the Glue Catalog, ETL jobs, and Athena workgroups, which shows a clear control plane for least-privilege access and governed query execution.

findings.title: Query and dashboard path preserves in-place analytics
findings.explanation: Athena reads curated S3 objects through catalog metadata and QuickSight sits on top of Athena, so the design avoids an unnecessary warehouse copy while still enabling visualization.

findings.title: Operational visibility is embedded in the existing services
findings.explanation: CloudWatch receives Athena scan, queueing, access-denial, Glue job, schema, and partition-health signals, providing enough observability for the described exercise without adding a separate monitoring stack.

results.summary: A coherent AWS data lake design using S3, Glue, Lake Formation, Athena, and QuickSight covers ingestion, cataloging, direct SQL querying, governance, and dashboarding with good support for large-scale use.

findings.title: Direct-query lake pattern is coherent and covers the core analytics path
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates ingestion, raw storage, curated storage, cataloging, governed SQL, and visualization. Athena reads curated S3 data directly, which matches the core 'query without moving it' requirement.

findings.title: Automated metadata discovery is well supported
findings.explanation: Glue Crawlers are used on both raw and curated prefixes and publish updates into the Glue Data Catalog, giving a concrete automation path for schema and partition discovery.

findings.title: Governing and restricting access is explicitly modeled
findings.explanation: Lake Formation is connected to the catalog, Glue ETL, and Athena, so the design shows where fine-grained authorization is enforced for both processing and querying.

results.summary: The design covers ingestion, cataloging, in-place SQL query, governance, and visualization with a coherent S3/Glue/Athena/QuickSight lake pattern.

findings.title: In-place query path preserves lake data locality
findings.explanation: Athena reads curated S3 objects directly through Glue Catalog metadata, which matches the core requirement to query data without moving it and supports the cost-minimizing access pattern.

findings.title: Governed fine-grained access model is explicit
findings.explanation: Lake Formation is wired to the catalog and Athena, with descriptions calling out least-privilege grants and column/row-filter permissions, which directly addresses sensitive-data control.

findings.title: Automated metadata discovery and publishing are well covered
findings.explanation: The combination of Glue Crawlers and ETL metadata publication gives two paths for catalog updates, which strengthens dataset discoverability and operational freshness.

results.summary: The design cleanly supports real-time score updates, low-latency leaderboard reads, periodic season resets, rank lookups, and anti-cheat controls using a coherent Kinesis/DynamoDB/Redis pipeline.

findings.title: Multi-layer anti-abuse and authorization path is well separated
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates WAF filtering, API authentication/authorization, scoped rate limiting, and score-result validation. That makes the trust boundaries clear and helps prevent client-authored score tampering from reaching durable state.

findings.title: Read path is optimized for instant top-player and rank queries
findings.explanation: Redis sorted sets are used directly for bounded top-K and rank lookups, while the read service keeps friend and global scopes separate. This is a strong fit for the low-latency retrieval requirement.

findings.title: Event-sourced projection supports replay and recovery
findings.explanation: Validated score events are durably written to Kinesis, projected into DynamoDB and Redis, and failures are isolated in a DLQ. This supports recovery, idempotency, and rebuilds from source events.

results.summary: The design presents a coherent AWS leaderboard architecture with authenticated score ingestion, ordered projection, Redis-backed low-latency reads, seasonal resets, and durable persistence for global and friend-based rankings.

findings.title: Strong end-to-end write-to-read flow for leaderboard updates
findings.explanation: The submission shows a coherent path from trusted game servers through validation, durable eventing, projection, and low-latency Redis reads. This directly supports the core real-time leaderboard behavior and the friend/global ranking access patterns.

findings.title: Clear separation of trust, abuse control, and game-result validation
findings.explanation: The design separates WAF, authentication, rate limiting, and score validation into distinct layers, which is a strong fit for protecting authenticated leaderboard writes without conflating transport abuse filtering with anti-cheat logic.

findings.title: Season rotation and historical retention are explicitly modeled
findings.explanation: The season coordinator updates the active season boundary and namespace while preserving history in DynamoDB, which supports periodic resets without losing past leaderboard data.

results.summary: The design provides a coherent AWS leaderboard architecture with trusted-score ingestion, Redis-backed instant reads, durable persistence, season rotation, anti-cheat controls, and monitoring for high-scale operation.

findings.title: Redis-backed read path matches the instant leaderboard retrieval goal
findings.explanation: The read service queries Redis sorted sets for top-K and rank lookups, which is the right architectural choice for very low-latency leaderboard reads.

findings.title: End-to-end score pipeline supports real-time updates with durable replay
findings.explanation: Trusted game-server submissions flow through authentication, validation, durable stream publication, and idempotent projection into both DynamoDB and Redis. That sequence supports fast user-visible updates while preserving replayability and recovery.

findings.title: Season rotation is explicitly modeled rather than treated as a cache flush
findings.explanation: The Season Rotation Coordinator persists the new boundary and switches the active namespace, which is a robust way to reset leaderboards periodically while preserving historical data.

results.summary: The design is broadly coherent for a real-time AWS leaderboard, with strong ingestion, projection, persistence, and reset flows, but the read-path latency guarantee and friend-based ranking behavior need tighter definition.

findings.title: Read-path latency is not tightly bounded for the published sub-10ms target
findings.explanation: The design routes reads through a Lambda-based read service and allows DynamoDB fallback for friend-scope data. That is coherent, but it leaves cold-start and tail-latency behavior unspecified, so the architecture does not fully demonstrate that all read paths stay under the 10ms constraint.
findings.recommendation: Use provisioned concurrency or an always-on read tier for hot paths, and define a strict fallback policy so only bounded, latency-safe lookups execute on the critical read path.

findings.title: Friend-based rankings are only partially defined
findings.explanation: The read service states it can combine caller-authorized friend scores when the friend set is bounded. That supports friend boards for small scopes, but it does not fully specify how global friend rankings behave for large or unbounded friend sets, which is a core requirement gap.
findings.recommendation: Define the friend-board retrieval strategy for large friend graphs, such as precomputed friend views, paginated fan-out, or a bounded eligibility policy with explicit limits.

findings.title: Real-time ingestion path is well separated from abuse control
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates WAF filtering, authentication, rate limiting, and score validation, which reduces the chance that abuse handling blocks legitimate game-result processing.

findings.title: Season reset is handled idempotently without destructive rewrites
findings.explanation: A season coordinator persists the new boundary and switches the active namespace instead of deleting historical data, which is a robust approach for periodic leaderboard resets.

results.summary: A coherent Azure IoT design with scalable device onboarding, partitioned telemetry ingestion, real-time processing, durable command handling, and five-year archive retention.

findings.title: End-to-end device lifecycle is well integrated
findings.explanation: Device enrollment, lifecycle event projection, and operator-visible metadata are connected in a coherent control plane that supports fleet operations without conflating telemetry with inventory updates.

findings.title: Telemetry and command paths are cleanly separated
findings.explanation: High-volume sensor traffic stays on the IoT Hub/stream-processing path, while commands use a durable queue and authenticated operations API. That separation supports scale and reduces control-plane coupling.

findings.title: Five-year retention is handled by a durable archive, not the hot query store alone
findings.explanation: The design correctly distinguishes bounded query access from long-term retention by using Blob/Data Lake for the governed record while keeping the query store as a hot projection.

results.summary: The design gives a coherent Azure IoT platform with explicit device provisioning, high-scale ingestion, real-time stream processing, anomaly detection, command delivery, telemetry visualization, lifecycle management, and five-year retention coverage.

findings.title: End-to-end device operations and telemetry paths are well separated
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates the high-volume ingest path, lifecycle metadata path, telemetry query path, and operator command path, which reduces coupling and makes the overall flow easier to reason about.

findings.title: Scale strategy is explicitly tied to hub quotas and partitioned downstream processing
findings.explanation: The architecture does not assume a single ingestion point; it calls out IoT Hub quota validation, stable device assignment, partitioned telemetry streaming, and separate lifecycle routing to handle the published 10M+ / 1M+ scale targets.

findings.title: Retention and auditability are addressed with a durable archive plus observability
findings.explanation: The five-year archive is paired with completeness and integrity monitoring, which strengthens long-term data stewardship beyond a simple storage declaration.

results.summary: A coherent Azure IoT platform design covers device enrollment, high-rate telemetry ingestion, real-time processing, five-year retention, anomaly detection, command delivery, dashboarding, and lifecycle management with clear data/control-plane separation.

findings.title: Strong end-to-end IoT control and telemetry path
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates device enrollment, authenticated telemetry ingestion, stream processing, anomaly detection, command delivery, and lifecycle projection. This gives a coherent path for both data plane and control plane behavior.

findings.title: Scalable multi-service partitioning is explicitly considered
findings.explanation: The submission avoids assuming a single hub or a single store can handle all load, and instead calls out stable device assignment, partitioned telemetry, and a separate archive path. That matches the published scale intent well.

results.summary: A coherent Azure IoT platform design that covers device onboarding, high-rate telemetry ingestion, real-time processing, anomaly detection, long-term retention, commands, visualization, and lifecycle management with clear scaling and governance choices.

findings.title: Comprehensive end-to-end IoT pipeline coverage
findings.explanation: The submission covers device enrollment, telemetry ingestion, stream processing, anomaly detection, long-term retention, command delivery, lifecycle management, dashboard access, and observability with coherent Azure-native components and connections.

results.summary: The architecture covers device onboarding, high-volume telemetry ingest, real-time processing, anomaly detection, long-term retention, device commands, telemetry visualization, and lifecycle management with a coherent Azure-oriented flow.

findings.title: Per-device trust and lifecycle controls are well separated

findings.title: Telemetry path is coherent for scale and low-latency processing
findings.explanation: The direct device-to-IoT Hub ingest path, partitioned stream processing, and bounded hot query store form a coherent pipeline for high-rate telemetry and sub-five-second analytics.

findings.title: Explicit observability covers the operational critical path
findings.explanation: Monitoring is attached to ingress, processing, query, archive, and command paths, which gives the design visibility into latency, throttling, retention, and command health without requiring extra standalone observability components.

results.summary: A coherent Azure serverless REST API design with edge JWT validation, consumer throttling, cache-aside reads, Cosmos-backed CRUD, and broad telemetry support for the stated scope.

findings.title: Clear gateway-to-function split with auth and throttling at the edge
findings.explanation: The design places JWT validation, request validation, TLS termination, and consumer throttling in API Management, then repeats authorization in the Function layer before data access. That separation supports both security and operational simplicity.

findings.title: Cache-aside flow is scoped to preserve correctness
findings.explanation: Redis is used only for eligible read routes, with keys scoped by resource and authorization dimensions and invalidation after durable writes. This avoids making the cache the source of truth and reduces stale/cross-tenant risk.

findings.title: Telemetry covers the main latency and failure paths
findings.explanation: Application Insights receives gateway status/throttle/duration data, Function spans including cold starts and dependencies, and downstream Cosmos/Redis health signals. That is enough to understand where latency and errors originate.

results.summary: A coherent Azure serverless REST API design covers REST routing, CRUD handlers, JWT auth, throttling, cache-aside reads, and end-to-end telemetry with sensible service boundaries.

findings.title: Cache-aside read path with scoped invalidation

findings.title: Observability spans the full request path
findings.explanation: Application Insights receives traces and metrics from APIM, Functions, Cosmos DB, and Redis, which provides the necessary visibility for latency, throttling, dependency timing, and error analysis.

findings.title: Cache-aside read path with scoped invalidation

findings.title: Correlated telemetry across gateway, function, database, and cache

results.summary: The design cleanly maps REST, CRUD, JWT auth, throttling, caching, and monitoring onto APIM, Azure Functions, Cosmos DB, Redis, and Application Insights with coherent end-to-end flows.

results.summary: A coherent Azure serverless REST API design with edge JWT validation, consumer throttling, cache-aside reads, Cosmos-backed CRUD, and broad telemetry support for the stated scope.

findings.title: Cache-aside flow is scoped to preserve correctness
findings.explanation: Redis is used only for eligible read routes, with keys scoped by resource and authorization dimensions and invalidation after durable writes. This avoids making the cache the source of truth and reduces stale/cross-tenant risk.

findings.title: Telemetry covers the main latency and failure paths
findings.explanation: Application Insights receives gateway status/throttle/duration data, Function spans including cold starts and dependencies, and downstream Cosmos/Redis health signals. That is enough to understand where latency and errors originate.

results.summary: The design is broadly coherent for a real-time AWS leaderboard, with strong ingestion, projection, persistence, and reset flows, but the read-path latency guarantee and friend-based ranking behavior need tighter definition.

findings.title: Read-path latency is not tightly bounded for the published sub-10ms target
findings.explanation: The design routes reads through a Lambda-based read service and allows DynamoDB fallback for friend-scope data. That is coherent, but it leaves cold-start and tail-latency behavior unspecified, so the architecture does not fully demonstrate that all read paths stay under the 10ms constraint.
findings.recommendation: Use provisioned concurrency or an always-on read tier for hot paths, and define a strict fallback policy so only bounded, latency-safe lookups execute on the critical read path.

findings.title: Friend-based rankings are only partially defined
findings.explanation: The read service states it can combine caller-authorized friend scores when the friend set is bounded. That supports friend boards for small scopes, but it does not fully specify how global friend rankings behave for large or unbounded friend sets, which is a core requirement gap.
findings.recommendation: Define the friend-board retrieval strategy for large friend graphs, such as precomputed friend views, paginated fan-out, or a bounded eligibility policy with explicit limits.

findings.title: Real-time ingestion path is well separated from abuse control
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates WAF filtering, authentication, rate limiting, and score validation, which reduces the chance that abuse handling blocks legitimate game-result processing.

findings.title: Season reset is handled idempotently without destructive rewrites
findings.explanation: A season coordinator persists the new boundary and switches the active namespace instead of deleting historical data, which is a robust approach for periodic leaderboard resets.

results.summary: The design covers the ML deployment pipeline end to end with versioned training, registry-backed promotion, A/B serving, monitoring, and automated retraining; remaining gaps are mainly in cost control, trigger specificity, and operational clarity.

findings.title: Autoscaling strategy is present but not explicitly bounded for the requested throughput
findings.explanation: The endpoint autos-scales on request load and saturation, which is directionally correct for 1000+ predictions/sec, but the submission does not specify scaling limits, instance sizing, or concurrency behavior that would show how the design stays stable at that load.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit scaling policy details such as target metrics, min/max capacity, and concurrency assumptions so the throughput target is operationally credible.

findings.title: Warm-capacity inference strategy may raise serving cost
findings.explanation: The endpoint is intentionally kept warm for the latency objective and can split traffic across variants. That supports performance, but it also implies ongoing capacity spend that is not balanced with an explicit cost-control mechanism for low-traffic periods.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit cost-aware serving policy such as scale-to-zero for noncritical environments, scheduled warm-capacity tuning, or variant right-sizing based on observed load.

findings.title: Inference path depends on an assumed low-overhead API front door
findings.explanation: API Gateway fronts the prediction path and forwards to the endpoint, which is coherent, but the design does not spell out how request validation, serialization, and backend invocation overhead stay within the under-100ms budget under peak load.
findings.recommendation: Specify payload limits, connection reuse, and timeout budgets for the API-to-endpoint path so the latency target remains credible at peak traffic.

findings.title: Security posture is implied rather than fully spelled out
findings.explanation: The API is described as authenticated and validated, and S3 uses access-controlled versioned prefixes with encryption, but the endpoint- and registry-side access boundaries are not described in the same level of detail.
findings.recommendation: Clarify IAM/service-role boundaries for registry updates and endpoint invocation so the trust model is explicit end to end.

findings.title: Retraining trigger conditions need operational definition
findings.explanation: Monitoring can start qualified retraining, but the design does not state the drift or schedule thresholds that determine when retraining is triggered, which makes the automation path partially underspecified.
findings.recommendation: Define the retraining trigger policy, including drift thresholds, alert routing, and any debounce or approval rules.

findings.title: Deployment automation is gated but rollback behavior is not explicit
findings.explanation: The workflow can apply a reviewed endpoint configuration after checks pass, but the submission does not describe what happens when deployment or post-deployment validation fails, which leaves the automation path incomplete.
findings.recommendation: Specify rollback and failed-deployment handling, including how the registry rollback reference is used to restore the prior serving version.

findings.title: A/B traffic split criteria are not fully parameterized
findings.explanation: The endpoint supports traffic splitting for comparison, but the submission does not describe how split ratios are selected, rolled back, or promoted based on experiment outcomes.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit traffic-split and promotion rules, including rollback conditions and success metrics, to make A/B testing operationally complete.

findings.title: Monitoring coverage is good but alert actionability is not explicit
findings.explanation: CloudWatch metrics include latency, errors, saturation, variant metrics, and drift indicators, which is a strong observability foundation; however, the alerting/decision thresholds that turn metrics into actions are not detailed.
findings.recommendation: Define alarm thresholds, dashboards, and which metric combinations trigger retraining or rollback to make operations more actionable.

findings.title: Serve-and-compare architecture is appropriate for the requested scale
findings.explanation: The multi-variant endpoint with autoscaling and warm capacity directly addresses the need to scale inference endpoints while preserving fast comparison traffic.

findings.title: Lineage is captured end to end across data, code, and artifacts
findings.explanation: The registry and experiment store preserve run IDs, digests, evaluation evidence, and rollback references, which supports lineage and repeatability well.
